325	### Manual filtering: file types
326	
327	Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
328	For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
329	want to see results for Rust files:
330	
331	```
332	$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
333	```
334	
335	Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
336	file types:
337	
338	```
339	$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
340	```
341	
342	or, more succinctly,
343	
344	```
345	$ rg 'fn run' -trust
346	```
347	
348	The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
349	assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
350	write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
351	example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
352	files and C header files:
353	
354	```
355	$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
356	```
357	
358	or you could just use the C file type:
359	
360	```
361	$ rg 'int main' -tc
362	```
363	
364	Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:
365	
366	```
367	$ rg clap --type-not rust
368	```
369	
370	or, more succinctly,
371	
372	```
373	$ rg clap -Trust
374	```
375	
376	That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
377	files of this type."
378	
379	To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:
380	
381	```
382	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
383	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
384	```
385	
386	By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
387	types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
388	types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
389	consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:
390	
391	```
392	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
393	```
394	
395	or, more succinctly,
396	
397	```
398	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
399	```
400	
401	The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
402	`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
403	the pattern `title`. If you ran
404	
405	```
406	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
407	```
408	
409	Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
410	part of ripgrep's built-in types.
411	
412	It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
413	current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
414	persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
415	then you should either create a shell alias:
416	
417	```
418	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
419	```
420	
421	or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
422	([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)
423	
424	#### The special `all` file type
425	
426	A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
427	for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
428	including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
429	to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
430	stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.
431	
432	As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
433	`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
434	Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
435	`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
436	by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
437	other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
438	`my-shell-library.bash`.

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering searches by file type in ripgrep

When you search all day, you rarely want every file. You want the Rust, or the
Python, or everything except the minified JavaScript. ripgrep gives each file
format a short name and lets you filter on that name instead of retyping globs.
This guide covers the four flags that make it work: `--type`, `--type-not`,
`--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` (`-t`): keep only one kind of file

A file type is a name assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant
files. Instead of spelling out the extensions:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

you name the type:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form `-t` takes the type name with no space, so `-trust` reads as
"type rust." One name can stand in for a whole family of extensions. C source
and header files, for instance, both live under the `c` type, so `-tc` replaces
`-g '*.{c,h}'`.

You can pass `--type` more than once, and the results are combined: `rg -trust
-tpython` searches both. One caveat on precedence: `--type` ranks *below* both
the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files. A `.gitignore` entry or
an explicit `--glob` can still exclude a file your type would otherwise match.

## `--type-not` (`-T`): exclude a kind of file

The mirror image excludes a type. To search everything but Rust:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." The two compose: `rg -Trust -ttoml -Tjson` includes TOML while
excluding Rust and JSON.

### The special `all` type

Both flags accept the value `all`. `--type all` behaves as if you had passed
`--type` for every type ripgrep knows about, including any you added on the
command line. This is "whitelist" mode: ripgrep only searches files it
recognizes through a type definition. Conversely, `--type-not all` is
"blacklist" mode: only files that match *no* known type are searched.

The difference is sharper than it looks. Suppose your directory holds
`my-shell-script` (no extension) and `my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type
sh` and `rg --type all` search only `my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh`
type's globs match extensions, not bare names. But `rg --type-not all` searches
`my-shell-script` and skips `my-shell-library.bash`, since only the unextended
file is unrecognized.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known open
formats. To see them all, with the globs behind each one:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as a name, a colon, then a comma-delimited list
of its globs. Pipe it back through ripgrep to inspect one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

`--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same
command line, so it is also how you confirm a custom type came out the way you
meant.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

When you keep reaching for the same group of formats, name it. Say you search
"web" files, meaning HTML, CSS, and JavaScript:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` adds exactly one glob, so repeat the flag to build the type
up; or fold them into a single brace glob:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Defining a type and using it are separate steps. `--type-add 'web:...'` only
creates the name; `-tweb` then filters with it. The added globs join ripgrep's
built-in types rather than replacing them. Type names must be made of Unicode
letters or numbers only, with no punctuation.

You can also compose types from existing ones with the `include` directive,
listing other type names separated by commas:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
```

That makes `src` match C++, Python, and Markdown files at once. You can still
add more globs to it afterward with another `--type-add 'src:*.foo'`.

To start a type from scratch, `--type-clear NAME` drops every glob previously
defined for it; you can then add fresh globs after the clear.

### Nothing is saved

`--type-add` and `--type-clear` apply only to the command that carries them.
Type settings are not persisted. To make a custom type available everywhere,
put it in a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file so
every invocation picks it up.
"}

- **The `--type-list` output format** (name, colon, comma-delimited globs) and the fact that it reflects `--type-add`/`--type-clear` are from `TypeList`'s `doc_long`; the built-in "large set of well-known open formats" framing matches the header comment in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`.
